extracted.intended_audience: aspiring joke writers and novice comedians
extracted.subtask_description: Practical step-by-step guidance for generating, structuring, editing, and testing short jokes and one-liners (idea generation, setup/punchline construction, joke formulas, word choice, and timing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brainstorm topics from your daily life
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate topics drawn from ordinary daily experiences (examples given: airports, dating, parents, jobs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with relatable, everyday topics as raw material for jokes; the page suggests listing such areas to seed associations and ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify an opinion or strong feeling about the topic
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a clear opinion or strong feeling (anger, confusion, frustration are recommended) about the chosen topic to anchor the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy often arises from a recognizable emotional stance — pick a strong reaction or viewpoint and use it as the joke's angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a list of associations (10–20 words/phrases)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each topic, write 10–20 associated words or phrases to expand possible angles and imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large association lists increase the chance of unexpected pairings or surprising links; treat this as an ideation exercise rather than polishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for unexpected pairings or absurd contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Scan your association list for surprising juxtapositions or logical/semantic contradictions that could become punchlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page frames this as a discovery step: absurd or incongruous combinations often produce comedic tension to exploit in a setup/punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: The setup creates an expectation (use plain, direct language)
rubrics_metrics.description: The setup should establish a single, clear expectation for the audience using straightforward, plain language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep setups direct and unambiguous so the audience forms a predictable line of thought that the punchline can later subvert. The rubric phrasing: 'Does the setup raise a single, clear expectation?'

rubrics_metrics.name: The punchline breaks/subverts the expectation (surprising and inevitable)
rubrics_metrics.description: The punchline must break the expectation the setup created; the break should be both surprising and feel inevitable in retrospect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a balance where the audience is surprised but, after hearing it, recognizes why the punchline fits. The rubric asks: 'Does the punchline subvert that expectation?' and emphasizes surprise + inevitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinterpretation (second meaning) — make the audience reread the setup
rubrics_metrics.description: The punchline should introduce a second meaning or frame that makes the audience reinterpret the setup in a new light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Called the 'reinterpretation' rule on the page; the explicit rubric item: 'Is there a "second meaning" that makes the audience reread the setup?' This is central to satisfying a strong twist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place the funniest word at the very end of the punchline
rubrics_metrics.description: Position the single funniest/strongest word at the end of the punchline for maximum impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide repeatedly advises terminal word placement as a structural trick to maximize punch. This is also reflected in the rubric: 'Is the funniest word at the end?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Triple formula (A, B, C — C subverts AB pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a three-item pattern where the third item breaks the pattern established by the first two (A, B, then subversive C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Triple is a classic comedic structure: set two parallel items then break expectation with the third. Useful for rhythm and surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the List formula (list-of-three with the third item absurd)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a list (commonly three items) where the final item is absurd or incongruous compared to the prior items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists, especially of three, build a predictable rhythm so the last absurd item lands harder; the page highlights list-of-three as a reliable form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Comparison formula ("X is like Y" with an unexpected Y)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame a simile or analogy where the 'Y' is unexpected, reframing X in a humorous light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons work by connecting two domains; making the second domain surprising produces humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Reframe (describe a familiar thing as if alien)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe something ordinary as though it's strange or alien to reveal absurdity and generate laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defamiliarization/reframing shifts perspective and uncovers comedic detail; it's presented as one of several reliable joke formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Misdirection (lead audience one way, land elsewhere)
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure the setup to guide the audience's expectations to one interpretation, then direct the punchline to a different target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misdirection is a fundamental comedic mechanism; the setup primes an interpretation that the punchline undercuts or redirects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut every word that isn't essential (every word should be load-bearing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove any word that doesn't contribute meaningfully to the setup or punchline; if the joke is understandable without the word, delete it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concision sharpens jokes: the page advises pruning ruthlessly. The rubric echoes this: 'Is every word load-bearing?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Replace soft words with hard, specific ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer concrete, specific nouns and verbs over vague or soft language (examples: 'dog' beats 'a small mammal'; 'Buick' beats 'car').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specificity paints clearer mental images and often increases comedic payoff; the guide gives explicit replacement examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test the joke on a friend; if you have to explain, rewrite
rubrics_metrics.description: Try the joke with someone else — if it requires explanation to land, it needs rewriting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple audience-testing as a quality filter. The page advises live feedback: rewrite any joke that must be explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing/delivery — most one-liners should land in under 8–10 seconds
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful of pacing; the guide recommends most one-liners land in under 8 seconds (the final rubric asks whether it 'lands in under 10 seconds').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time your delivery during edits and rehearsals. The guide gives both 'under 8 seconds' (method) and 'under 10 seconds' (final checklist), indicating a short tight window for one-liners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Someone you trust laughs without explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple pass/fail audience criterion: a trusted listener should laugh without needing an explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the social test of joke readiness, presented explicitly in the 'Is This Joke Done?' rubric: 'Does someone you trust laugh without explanation?' Use it as a final sanity check.
